        Choosing a radio & licensesWhich radio, GMRS legality, getting licensed
        Which radio should I use?Quick decision guide
        • Family, no license, simplest: FRS bubble-pack radios. Short range, but anyone can use them.
        • Family and neighbors, longer range, repeaters: a GMRS handheld (TIDRADIO TD-H3 GMRS, Baofeng UV-5G/UV-5X, Wouxun, Midland, etc.) plus a $35 license that covers your relatives.
        • Most capability and organized emergency help: ham radio (Baofeng UV-5R, TIDRADIO TD-H8 ham version, etc.) with a Technician license.
        • On the highway: CB in the vehicle (Ch 19 traffic, Ch 9 emergency).
        • Just listening (weather, aircraft, local news): a multi-band receiver. The TD-H3 also receives AM airband.

        Many prepared families use GMRS for the family + ham for the wider community. Pick one plan and have everyone practice it.

        Is my radio legal for GMRS?The Part 95 rule everyone gets wrong

        To transmit on GMRS, the radio itself must be FCC-certified for GMRS (Part 95E). A license alone isn't enough.

        RadioGMRS transmit?Notes
        Baofeng UV-5R, BF-F8HP, most "ham" BaofengsNoNot Part 95 certified. Legal on ham bands with a ham license. It will physically transmit on GMRS, but that's not allowed.
        Baofeng UV-5X / UV-5G, UV-5G PlusYesGMRS-certified versions of the UV-5R design. Transmit only on GMRS.
        TIDRADIO TD-H3 GMRS versionYes22 GMRS + 8 repeater channels, NOAA, multi-band receive including airband.
        TIDRADIO TD-H8 GMRS versionYesBigger, more powerful. Power is limited in GMRS mode.
        TIDRADIO TD-H3 / TD-H8 ham versionsHam bandsFor licensed hams on 2 m / 70 cm.

        How to check any radio: find the FCC ID on the label (under the battery) and search it at fccid.io or the FCC's equipment authorization site. Look for "Part 95E" (GMRS) or "Part 95B" (FRS) in the grant.

        "Unlocking" a GMRS radio to transmit on ham or MURS frequencies, or using a ham radio on GMRS, breaks the equipment rules. In a real life-threatening emergency, use what you have (see Emergency → legal).

        Get a GMRS license ($35, no exam, 10 years)Step by step on the FCC website
        1. Go to the FCC's CORES registration and create an FRN (FCC Registration Number). It's free.
        2. Log in to the FCC ULS (Universal Licensing System) License Manager with your FRN.
        3. Choose "Apply for a New License" and select ZA – General Mobile Radio (GMRS).
        4. Answer the questions, certify, and submit. Pay the $35 fee.
        5. Your call sign (like WSAB123) usually shows up within a day or two. Download your license from ULS.

        One license covers you and your immediate family members (spouse, children, grandchildren, stepchildren, parents, grandparents, stepparents, brothers, sisters, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and in-laws), at any age. You must be 18+ to apply.

        Write your call sign on a label on every family radio. Everyone uses the same call sign.

        Get a ham (amateur) licenseTechnician → General → Extra
        1. Study (in Learn → Exam prep) the Technician question pool (35-question exam; 26 correct to pass). A new question pool took effect July 1, 2026, so use 2026–2030 study material. Free practice tests: HamStudy.org, ARRL, and others.
        2. Find an exam session run by Volunteer Examiners (ARRL VEC, Laurel VEC, GLAARG). Many are in person; some are online. Exam fees are small and vary (some free).
        3. Get an FRN first and bring it to the exam.
        4. After you pass, pay the FCC's $35 application fee when you get the email from the FCC. Your call sign appears in ULS, usually within days.
        • Technician: all ham frequencies above 30 MHz (2 m, 70 cm, etc.) plus some HF (10 m voice). Enough for local emergency work and repeaters.
        • General: most HF bands, for statewide, national and worldwide contact without repeaters.
        • Extra: all amateur privileges.

        Then join a local club, ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service) or RACES, and check into weekly nets to practice.

        Guides for any radioCHIRP, identify a radio, weather alerts, airband
        Program with CHIRP (computer, recommended)Faster, fewer mistakes, easy backup

        Do this now while you have internet: install CHIRP (free, chirpmyradio.com) on a laptop and get a programming cable with a genuine FTDI chip (cheap clone cables often won't connect). TIDRADIO radios program over plain USB-C.

        1. Plug the cable firmly into the radio (Kenwood-style 2-pin jack on Baofeng; push until it clicks).
        2. CHIRP → Radio → Download from radio. Pick the port, brand and model.
        3. Save a backup file right away before changing anything.
        4. Edit the spreadsheet: Frequency, Name, Tone Mode (Tone = send a tone; TSQL = send and receive tone), Tone, Duplex (+, −, or blank), Offset, Mode (FM/NFM/AM), Power.
        5. Radio → Upload to radio. Then test a channel.
        6. Copy the same file to every family radio of the same model.

        CHIRP can also import repeater lists (RepeaterBook) while online. Do it before you need it and keep the saved files on your phone and laptop.

        Not listed? Identify any radioFCC ID, CHIRP, firmware rules
        1. Find the FCC ID on the label (under the battery). Search it at fcc.gov/oet/ea/fccid or fccid.io. "Part 95E" = GMRS, "Part 95B" = FRS, "Part 95J" = MURS. Ham radios usually show Part 15 only, since ham transmitters don't need certification.
        2. Check the CHIRP supported radios list (chirpmyradio.com) for the exact model. Never upload a file made for a different model.
        3. Get firmware and manuals only from the official manufacturer site. Firmware updates can brick radios: follow instructions exactly, with a full battery.
        4. Add it to Plan → My radios with your notes.
        Set up NOAA Weather Radio alertsGet warnings with no internet or cell service

        NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts National Weather Service forecasts and warnings 24/7 on 7 channels (162.400–162.550 MHz). It also carries other hazard alerts. A SAME alert radio wakes you with a siren only for warnings in your county.

        1. Find your nearest transmitter and its channel on weather.gov (NOAA Weather Radio coverage pages) now, while online. Pick the channel with the clearest signal at home.
        2. Look up your county's 6-digit SAME code (for example, 012095 is Orange County, Florida: "012" is the state, "095" the county). You can also call the NWS at 1-888-NWS-SAME (1-888-697-7263).
        3. Enter the channel and SAME code in your weather radio following its manual. Add nearby counties if storms often come from there.
        4. Put fresh backup batteries in the alert radio and keep it where you sleep.
        5. Write your channel and SAME code in My Radio Book.

        On handhelds: Baofeng, TIDRADIO and most GMRS radios receive NOAA channels, and many have a "weather alert" setting that watches for the 1050 Hz alert tone. They can't decode SAME county codes, so they alert for the whole transmitter area.

        How to hear pilots and towersAirband basics (118–137 MHz AM)
        • Aircraft voice uses AM, not FM. You need a radio that receives AM airband: TIDRADIO TD-H3, Quansheng UV-K5, or a scanner. The Baofeng UV-5R can't.
        • In the US, listening is legal. Transmitting is not unless you're a licensed aircraft or ground station; handheld GMRS/ham radios can't transmit there anyway.
        • Use the long antenna and go high. You'll hear aircraft in the sky from far away, but the ground side (tower, ground) only nearby.
        • Set squelch low (or press MONI) because aircraft calls are short.

        What you'll hear

        WhoWhat
        ATISRecorded loop: weather, runway in use, info letter ("information Bravo").
        Clearance / GroundRoute clearances and taxiing.
        TowerTakeoffs and landings.
        Approach / DepartureAircraft within ~30–50 miles of busy airports.
        CenterAirliners at altitude, en route.
        CTAF / UNICOMSmall airports without a tower; pilots announce their own positions.
        121.5 GuardEmergency. Also emergency locator transmitter (ELT) signals: a warbling siren sound.

        Words to know

        • Squawk 7700 = emergency, 7600 = lost radio contact, 7500 = hijack.
        • "Mayday" = distress, "Pan-Pan" = urgency.
        • "Heavy" = large aircraft. "Souls on board" = people aboard.
        • Altitudes: "flight level two-four-zero" = 24,000 ft. Headings in degrees, times in Zulu (UTC).

        Find your local airport frequencies while online (FAA Chart Supplement, AirNav) and save them in My Radio Book.

        Other popular radios worth knowingQuick notes
        • Quansheng UV-K5/K6: cheap ham handheld that also receives AM airband. Ham use only.
        • Wouxun KG-935G / KG-805G, Midland GXT/MXT, BTECH GMRS-PRO: GMRS-certified handhelds and mobiles.
        • Mobile (vehicle) GMRS or ham radios: 15–50 W with a roof antenna. Ranges can be several times a handheld's.
        • Yaesu, Icom, Kenwood: higher-end ham radios with better receivers; many support APRS and digital modes.
        Troubleshooting any radioNo audio, repeaters, transmit, range, programming, battery

        Work down each list in order and stop when the problem is fixed. These checks apply to almost any FM handheld or mobile; for menu names, use your model's guide or manual.

        No receive audio
        1. Volume up, accessories out. Unplug any speaker mic or earpiece; a half-seated plug can mute the speaker.
        2. Open the squelch. Press Monitor (or set squelch to 0). Hear hiss? Go to step 4. Total silence? Go to step 3.
        3. Silence even with squelch open points to the speaker, a stuck accessory jack, or a fault. Try an earpiece. If that works, the speaker or jack is the problem.
        4. Hiss but no voices: confirm the exact frequency or channel, and turn off any receive tone (CTCSS/DCS). A wrong receive tone keeps the radio silent even when others are talking.
        5. Check the mode. Airband needs AM; ham and GMRS voice is FM. Wide/narrow mismatch makes audio quiet or distorted.
        6. Prove the receiver works: tune a NOAA weather frequency. If you hear it, the radio is fine and nobody may be transmitting on your channel, or they're out of range.
        7. Antenna screwed on firmly and meant for this band.
        Can't access a repeater
        1. Do you hear the repeater's users? If not, check the output frequency, your receive tone, and whether you're in range. Fix receive first.
        2. Offset: direction and amount must match the listing. Common: 2 m ±600 kHz, 70 cm ±5 MHz, GMRS +5 MHz. Repeater offset calculator.
        3. Transmit tone: most repeaters need a CTCSS or DCS tone on your transmit. Tone mode must send it (often “Tone” or “TSQL”), and the value must match exactly.
        4. Kerchunk test: key up for 1 second, release, listen. A tail or courtesy beep means the repeater heard you. No tail: recheck offset and tone.
        5. Bandwidth: most ham and GMRS repeaters expect standard (wide) FM. Narrow can be quiet or ignored.
        6. Signal: high power, go higher or outside, use a better antenna.
        7. Busy-channel lockout can block your transmit while the repeater is still transmitting.
        8. Access rules: some GMRS repeaters are private and need the owner's permission and tone.
        Radio won't transmit
        1. Does the TX light or icon come on when you press PTT? If yes, skip to step 6.
        2. Is the frequency one this radio is allowed to transmit on? GMRS-certified radios refuse non-GMRS frequencies. Many ham radios block transmit outside the ham bands. Mobiles with a 5 W minimum can't transmit on FRS-only Ch 8–14.
        3. Channel settings: look for “RX only”, “TX inhibit” or busy-channel lockout on that channel.
        4. Battery: many radios refuse to transmit when the battery is low. Charge and retry.
        5. Time-out timer: if transmit cuts off after a set time, the TOT is doing its job. Release PTT and press again.
        6. TX light comes on but nobody hears you: the other radios may have a receive tone you're not sending. Match tones, or ask them to turn theirs off.
        7. Accessories: unplug the speaker mic; a faulty one can hold the radio in receive. Turn VOX off.
        8. Antenna: never transmit without one. If the radio got warm while transmitting with a bad antenna, stop and check it.
        Poor range
        1. Expect line of sight. Handheld to handheld at ground level is often a mile or two in town. Hills, buildings and vehicles block signals.
        2. Height beats power. Step outside, climb, stand on high ground, get away from metal.
        3. Antenna first. A longer, band-matched antenna often helps more than more watts. In a vehicle, an outside roof antenna makes a big difference. Antennas.
        4. Check SWR on vehicle and base antennas. SWR calculator.
        5. High power on, battery charged. Some radios lose power as the battery drops.
        6. Coax: long runs of thin cable eat signal, especially on UHF. Coax loss.
        7. Use a repeater if one covers both of you.
        Programming fails (cable, CHIRP or app)
        1. Right cable for this model. Plugs differ. Push Baofeng-style 2-pin plugs in firmly until they click fully home.
        2. Driver: cheap cables with counterfeit Prolific chips often fail. FTDI-chip cables are the reliable choice.
        3. Radio on, out of any menu, and the correct COM port picked in the software.
        4. Correct model selected. Newer firmware versions sometimes aren't supported by CHIRP yet; try the maker's software.
        5. Download first, save a backup file, then edit and upload. Keep the backup with your plan.
        6. Bluetooth/app: Bluetooth on, app permissions allowed (Android may ask for location to find Bluetooth devices), radio not connected to another phone.
        7. Still stuck: program the few emergency channels you need from the keypad if the model allows, and write them on a card.
        Battery or charging problems
        1. Seat the battery and clean the contacts with a dry cloth or pencil eraser.
        2. Charger light: read its color pattern in the manual. A flashing light can mean a fault or a battery too cold or hot to charge.
        3. USB-C won't charge? Some radio batteries don't charge from USB-C-to-C chargers. Try a USB-A-to-C cable and a basic 5 V charger.
        4. Drains fast: turn off dual watch, scan and long backlight, and use low power when close. Cold weather and old batteries cut capacity.
        5. Swollen, hot or leaking battery: stop using it and recycle it safely.
        6. For emergencies: keep a charged spare, an AA battery case if your model has one, and a car or USB charging option. Log charges in My radios.
        RadiosAntennas & gear

        Antennas, cables & gear

        The antenna and its height matter more than the radio's wattage. Here's what to buy, build and carry, and how to use it.

        The 3 rules of range

        1. Height beats power. Raising an antenna from 5 ft to 30 ft more than doubles line-of-sight distance. Doubling watts adds surprisingly little.
        2. A better antenna beats a bigger radio. A good antenna helps both transmit and receive. Extra power only helps transmit.
        3. VHF/UHF travel in line of sight. Hills, buildings and dense wet trees block them. Move to high, open ground.
        Handheld antennasThe cheapest big upgrade
        • Stock "rubber duck": short and convenient, but weak. Fine up close.
        • Aftermarket whip (e.g., Nagoya NA-771 style, ~15"): a popular, inexpensive upgrade for 2 m / 70 cm handhelds. Buy GMRS-tuned versions for GMRS radios.
        • Long "tactical" whip (~30"+): more gain, especially on VHF, but bulky and easy to break.
        • Roll-up J-pole / slim jim (ladder-line antenna): hang it high in a tree or from a window with a cord. A huge improvement over a duck, and it rolls up into a pocket.
        • Tiger tail / counterpoise: a ~19" wire attached at the antenna base and left hanging down. Cheap, often helps VHF noticeably.

        Hold the radio vertical. Both stations should use the same polarization (antennas vertical). Keep the antenna away from your head, car roof edges and metal.

        Connectors: buy the right oneSMA male vs female, BNC, PL-259, NMO
        • Look at the radio: if it has a threaded stud with a pin in the middle, it's SMA-male (Baofeng UV-5R style) → buy an SMA-female antenna. If the radio has threads around a hole, buy an SMA-male antenna.
        • BNC: push-and-twist bayonet, common on scanners.
        • PL-259 / SO-239 ("UHF" connector): big screw-on connectors on mobile radios, SWR meters and coax. PL-259 is the plug on the cable; SO-239 is the socket.
        • NMO: professional vehicle antenna mount (drilled or magnetic). Very common for GMRS and ham mobiles.
        • N-type: weatherproof, low-loss; used on better base antennas.

        Keep an adapter kit (SMA-F/M → SO-239, BNC, etc.) in your go-bag so any radio can connect to any antenna. Don't over-tighten SMA: finger-tight plus a tiny bit.

        Vehicle & base antennasWhere real range comes from
        • Magnetic mount: sticks to the roof in seconds, coax goes through the door gap. Center of the roof is best (the metal roof acts as the ground plane).
        • NMO through-roof or trunk-lip mount: best performance and permanent.
        • Base station: a vertical (ground plane, J-pole, or fiberglass collinear) as high as possible on a mast, roof or tree. Even 20–30 ft makes a dramatic difference.
        • Yagi (directional beam): points at a far repeater or a town; big gain in one direction. Tape-measure Yagis are a classic cheap build for 2 m.
        • Dual-band (2 m / 70 cm) antennas cover most ham work. GMRS needs a GMRS-tuned antenna (around 462–467 MHz); a 70 cm ham antenna often works OK but check SWR.
        • HF (ham General): wire dipoles or end-fed antennas hung between trees. Long wires, but cheap and they reach hundreds to thousands of miles.

        Stay far away from power lines when putting up any antenna or mast. If it falls, it must not be able to reach a line. Ground outdoor antennas and disconnect coax during lightning storms.

        Build a quarter-wave ground plane antennaA simple, strong base antenna from scraps
        1. Get an SO-239 chassis connector (square, 4-hole flange), stiff copper or brass wire (about 12 gauge), and a few small bolts.
        2. Use Tools → Antenna length to get the quarter-wave length for your frequency. Examples: 146 MHz ≈ 19.2", 462.6 MHz (GMRS) ≈ 6.1", 446 MHz ≈ 6.3".
        3. Solder the vertical wire into the center pin. Cut it slightly long; you'll trim it.
        4. Bolt 4 radials (each ~5–10% longer than the vertical) to the 4 flange holes. Bend them down at about 45°. That brings the antenna close to 50 ohms.
        5. Connect coax, check SWR at your frequency. If SWR is lowest below your frequency, the antenna is too long: trim a little at a time.
        6. Mount it as high as you can, vertical, and weatherproof the connector.
        Coax cable: choose by lengthLoss eats your signal before it leaves

        All coax loses some power. The loss grows with length and frequency, so UHF/GMRS suffers more than VHF. Use 50-ohm coax only.

        CableLoss per 100 ft @150 MHz@450 MHzUse
        RG-174 (thin)~8 dB~14 dBShort jumpers only
        RG-58~6.5 dB~11 dBUp to ~15–20 ft (mag mounts)
        RG-8X / mini-8~4.5 dB~8 dBUp to ~25–40 ft
        LMR-240~3 dB~5.3 dBMedium runs
        RG-213~2.8 dB~5 dBBase stations, rugged
        LMR-400~1.5 dB~2.7 dBLong runs, best of these

        Approximate figures; check your brand's spec sheet. 3 dB of loss = half your power gone, both transmitting and receiving. Try the coax loss calculator.

        • Keep runs as short as practical. Don't coil extra coax tightly, and don't kink or crush it (car door pinches, staples).
        • Seal outdoor connectors against water: wrap in electrical tape, then self-amalgamating (self-fusing) tape, then electrical tape again.
        SWR: what it means and how to check itIs your antenna matched?

        SWR (standing wave ratio) shows how well the antenna matches the radio. Power that isn't accepted by the antenna bounces back.

        SWRMeaning
        1.0–1.5Excellent
        1.5–2.0Good / acceptable
        2.0–3.0Poor. Fix if you can; use low power.
        3.0+Stop transmitting. Check connectors, cable and antenna. High SWR can damage the radio.

        Using an SWR meter (VHF/UHF type)

        1. Connect: radio → short jumper → meter "TX" port → meter "ANT" port → antenna coax.
        2. Set the radio to LOW power and a frequency you're licensed for (or a GMRS/ham channel on a legal radio).
        3. Set meter to FWD (forward), key up and adjust CAL to full scale (on cross-needle meters, just read where the needles cross).
        4. Switch to REF/SWR and key up briefly. Read SWR. Keep transmissions short and say your call sign.

        Using a NanoVNA (antenna analyzer)

        1. Calibrate it first (Open, Short, Load) over your frequency range, e.g., 140–150 MHz.
        2. Connect the antenna to port CH0. Display the SWR trace.
        3. The dip shows the antenna's best frequency. Lowest point below your frequency = antenna too long; above = too short.

        A NanoVNA doesn't transmit, so it's safe and legal to use on any frequency. It's the best ~$50–100 tool for building antennas.

        Power: batteries, solar, vehicleKeep radios alive for days
        • Spare batteries for every handheld, charged and labeled. Extended (3,800 mAh) Baofeng batteries are cheap.
        • AA battery case ("battery eliminator") for your radio model: runs on store-bought AA cells.
        • USB-C power bank + cable for radios with USB charging (TD-H3, many newer Baofengs). A 20,000 mAh bank recharges a handheld battery several times.
        • Car: a USB car charger or a 12 V "battery eliminator" that plugs into the cigarette lighter and replaces the battery pack.
        • Folding solar panel (20–100 W) to charge power banks or a 12 V LiFePO4 battery.
        • 12 V LiFePO4 battery (20–100 Ah) for mobile or base radios, with an inline fuse and Anderson Powerpole connectors (the ham standard).

        Always fuse the positive lead close to a 12 V battery. Lithium batteries can start fires if crushed, shorted or charged wrong. Use the correct charger.

        Tools to own and how to use themThe radio toolbox
        ToolWhat it's for / how to use
        Programming cable + laptop with CHIRPProgram all radios fast. Keep backups of each radio's file. Test the cable now.
        SWR meter (rated for VHF/UHF)Check antenna match before transmitting at high power. See SWR section.
        NanoVNATune homemade antennas; find bad cables.
        MultimeterCheck battery voltage, fuses, continuity in coax (center to center should beep; center to shield should not).
        Soldering iron (60 W+) + solderBuild antennas, fix cables, install PL-259 connectors.
        Coax stripper + crimperMake clean cable ends for crimp connectors.
        Adapter kitConnect any radio to any antenna.
        Self-amalgamating tape + electrical tapeWeatherproof outdoor connectors.
        Throw line + weight (paracord + throw bag)Get wire antennas high into trees, away from power lines.
        Zip ties, small tools, spare fusesField fixes.
        Earpiece / speaker micQuiet listening; keeps the radio on your belt and the antenna vertical.
        Notebook + pencilLog every message: time, who, what. Pencils write in cold and rain.
        Printed channel card (laminated)Works when phones die. Print this guide's Freq tab.
        Install a radio in your vehicleMobile GMRS or ham, step by step
        1. Plan: radio mounted where you can reach it without blocking airbags or vents; the mic within easy reach; the antenna on the center of the metal roof if possible.
        2. Power: for radios over ~10 W, run red and black leads directly to the battery through a rubber grommet in the firewall. Put an inline fuse on the positive lead within 18" of the battery (many installers fuse both leads). Use the wire gauge in the radio's manual.
        3. Antenna: magnetic mount (no holes, quick), trunk-lip or hatch mount, or an NMO through-roof mount (best). Route the coax under door seals and trim panels, not through pinch points.
        4. Check SWR at low power on a frequency you're licensed for. Trim or adjust the whip per its instructions.
        5. Program the radio the same as your handhelds so channel numbers match across the family.
        6. Noise: if you hear whine that changes with engine speed, check the power wiring goes straight to the battery and add ferrite chokes on the power leads.

        A 20–50 W mobile with a roof antenna often reaches several times farther than a handheld. It's the best upgrade for a family GMRS setup.

        Lightning protection & groundingProtect your home and gear
        • Disconnect outdoor antenna coax and unplug radios and power supplies when storms approach or you're away. That's the most reliable protection.
        • Install a coax lightning arrestor where the cable enters the house, connected to a ground rod.
        • Bond every ground rod (antenna, arrestor, house electrical ground) together with heavy wire. Separate, unbonded grounds can make lightning damage worse.
        • Keep ground wires short and straight, with no sharp bends.
        • Masts and towers should be grounded at the base. Follow the National Electrical Code (Article 810) or hire an electrician for permanent installs.
        • Never operate outdoors with a raised antenna during a thunderstorm.
        Radio go-bag checklistTap to check off · saved on this phone

        Learn radio

        BasicsGMRSHamExam prep

        The must-knows for any radio: how it works, how to talk on it, and how to plan for when everything else is down.

        Practice simulatorRehearse real calls, then practice out loud

        Rehearse real calls before you need them: pick what to say, see why, then practice saying it out loud with a hold-to-talk button. Uses your call sign from My plan if you've added one.

        The simulator needs JavaScript. The procedure words and message format below cover the same skills.

        Radio basics in 2 minutesFrequencies, channels, simplex, repeaters
        • A frequency (like 462.5625 MHz) is the exact "station". A channel is a saved shortcut to a frequency plus its settings.
        • Simplex: radio talks directly to radio on one frequency. Range is limited by line of sight: usually 1–5 miles for handhelds.
        • Repeater: a radio on a tower or hilltop that listens on one frequency (input) and re-transmits on another (output) at the same moment. A handheld can reach 20–50+ miles. You need the right offset and tone.
        • Half-duplex: only one person talks at a time. When you press PTT, you can't hear anyone else.
        • Squelch mutes static until a signal comes in. Too high and weak stations get cut off; too low and you hear constant hiss. Set it just above where hiss stops (Baofeng: 3–5).
        Tones, codes and "privacy" (CTCSS/DCS)Why you can't hear someone on the same channel
        • CTCSS (also called PL tone, "privacy code", sub-channel) is a low tone sent with your voice. DCS is a digital code that does the same job.
        • They are not private. Anyone with tones off hears you. They only stop your radio from opening for other people.
        • Repeaters usually require you to send a specific tone (e.g., 141.3 or 100.0) so they don't open for random noise.
        • If two radios are on the same channel and can't hear each other, check the tones first. In an emergency, set receive tones OFF.
        • Bubble-pack "Channel 20-22" means channel 20 with privacy code 22, not a different frequency. Codes 1–38 usually match the standard CTCSS list (see Tools).
        VHF vs UHF vs HFWhich band works where
        BandExamplesStrengthsWeak spots
        HF 3–30 MHzCB, ham 80/40/20 mBounces off the ionosphere: hundreds to thousands of miles without repeatersBig antennas, noise, changes with time of day
        VHF 30–300 MHzMURS, ham 2 m, marine, airband, NOAAOpen country, forests, farmland, over water; slightly farther than UHF in the openLonger antennas; struggles inside buildings
        UHF 300 MHz–3 GHzGMRS/FRS, ham 70 cmCities, inside buildings, short antennasMore blocked by hills and thick wet trees; more coax loss

        Modulation: FM is used by GMRS, FRS, MURS, 2 m / 70 cm ham, marine and NOAA. AM is used by airband and most CB. SSB (single sideband) is used for long-distance HF and CB channels 36–40 by convention.

        Wide vs narrow: mismatched bandwidth makes audio sound too quiet or too loud and distorted. GMRS main channels are wide (20 kHz); FRS and GMRS Ch 8–14 are narrow (12.5 kHz).

        How to make a callStep by step, with examples
        1. Listen first to make sure the channel is clear.
        2. Press PTT, wait a beat (repeaters need ~1 second to open), then speak.
        3. Say who you're calling, then who you are: "Dad, this is Jorge." On ham: "W1ABC, this is KD2XYZ."
        4. Wait for the reply. Keep each transmission short and end with "over" if it helps clarity.
        5. Pause a second between transmissions so anyone with emergency traffic can break in.
        6. End the conversation and identify: "KD2XYZ, clear." GMRS uses your GMRS call sign.
        "Mom, this is Jorge, over." "Jorge, Mom. Go ahead." "I'm at the school pickup. Roads are flooded on Main. Taking the bypass. Home in 30. Over." "Copy, bypass, home in 30. WSAB123. Out."
        • Ham: identify every 10 minutes during a conversation and at the end.
        • GMRS: identify every 15 minutes and at the end.
        • No call sign needed for FRS, MURS or CB.
        • No music, no profanity, no business ads on ham or GMRS. Plain language, no secret codes (on ham).
        Prowords: the words that matterOver, out, roger, say again…
        WordMeaning
        OVERI'm done talking; your turn to reply.
        OUTI'm done; conversation ended, no reply expected. ("Over and out" is a contradiction.)
        ROGER / COPYI received and understood your last message.
        WILCOI understand and will comply.
        SAY AGAINRepeat your last message. (Not "repeat": in some services that means something else.)
        I SAY AGAINI am repeating what I just said.
        READ BACKRepeat this message back to me so I know it's right.
        I SPELLI'll spell the next word phonetically.
        CORRECTIONI made an error; here's the correct version.
        STAND BY / WAITPause; I'll come back to you shortly.
        GO AHEADSend your message.
        AFFIRMATIVE / NEGATIVEYes / no. Clearer than yes/no on a noisy channel.
        BREAKSeparates parts of a message. "Break, break" = I need to interrupt with priority traffic.
        MAYDAYLife-threatening distress. Everyone else stops transmitting.
        PAN-PANUrgent, but no immediate danger to life.
        SÉCURITÉSafety information follows (weather, hazard).
        RADIO CHECKHow do you hear me? Reply: "loud and clear", "weak but readable", "broken".
        CLEARFinished and leaving the channel (ham: "KD2XYZ clear").
        73Ham shorthand for "best regards", used when signing off.
        Phonetic alphabet & numbersSpell anything clearly
        AAlfa
        BBravo
        CCharlie
        DDelta
        EEcho
        FFoxtrot
        GGolf
        HHotel
        IIndia
        JJuliett
        KKilo
        LLima
        MMike
        NNovember
        OOscar
        PPapa
        QQuebec
        RRomeo
        SSierra
        TTango
        UUniform
        VVictor
        WWhiskey
        XX-ray
        YYankee
        ZZulu

        Numbers: say each digit. 0 = "zero", 9 = "niner". 146.520 = "one-four-six point five-two-zero". Time in 24-hour format: 3:30 PM = "fifteen-thirty".

        Full page with pronunciation, Morse, a speller and the history: NATO alphabet. Also the Spell-it tool in Tools.

        Emergency message formatPass complete information every time

        When passing information for someone else (to a shelter, a net, 911), write it down in this order. It matches the spirit of the ICS-213 form used by emergency managers.

        1. To / From (names, agencies, call signs)
        2. Date & time (24-hour)
        3. Location (address, cross streets, GPS, landmarks)
        4. Situation (what happened, current conditions)
        5. People (how many, injuries, special needs)
        6. Needs (what, how much, how urgent)
        7. Callback (when and on what channel you'll be listening)

        Read it back. Keep the paper. A log of messages is gold for responders later.

        Nets: how to check inPractice now, be ready later

        A net is a scheduled, organized on-air meeting run by a net control station (NCS). Most ham clubs and many GMRS groups run weekly nets on a repeater. In disasters, nets organize traffic.

        1. Listen to the net's opening; NCS explains how to check in.
        2. When NCS calls for check-ins, say your call sign phonetically: "Kilo Delta Two X-ray Yankee Zulu." Add "with traffic" if you have a message.
        3. Wait to be acknowledged. Don't transmit unless NCS calls you, except for emergency traffic.
        4. Ask permission before leaving: "KD2XYZ, request to secure."

        Weekly nets are the best practice you can get. Write your local net times in My Radio Book.

        Build a family communication plan (PACE)Decide now, not during the disaster

        Military and emergency planners use PACE: a Primary, Alternate, Contingency and Emergency way to communicate. Example for a family:

        MethodExample
        PrimaryCell phone / textText first; texts get through when calls don't.
        AlternateGMRS simplexCh 17, no tones, at home and nearby.
        ContingencyGMRS repeaterLocal repeater on RP20, tone 141.3, for across town.
        EmergencyMeet-up point + 3-3-3Grandma's house; radio check at the top of every 3rd hour.
        • Pick an out-of-area contact everyone texts or calls (long-distance often works when local is jammed).
        • Pick meeting places: one near home, one outside the neighborhood.
        • Give kids a laminated card with names, call sign, channels and meeting places.
        • Practice monthly: a radio check on your channels. Fix what fails.

        Save your plan in the Plan tab.

        Texting and GPS when phones are downMeshtastic, GMRS data, APRS, Winlink, JS8Call

        Short text messages often get through when voice can't, and you can read them later. These are the main options:

        SystemLicenseWhat it does
        Meshtastic (LoRa mesh)NoneCheap pocket radios (~$30+) pair with your phone over Bluetooth. You type in the Meshtastic app; messages and GPS positions hop node to node with no cell service or internet. In the US it runs license-free around 915 MHz (902–928 MHz). Text only, about 200 characters per message.
        GMRS text / GPS radiosGMRSThe FCC allows short text messages and GPS location data on GMRS. Some GMRS radios send location and texts to matching radios.
        APRS (144.390)HamPosition, weather and short messages over 2 m. Digipeaters relay across a region.
        WinlinkHamReal email over radio, including attachments and ICS forms. Reaches gateway stations that connect to the internet somewhere else, or goes radio-to-radio.
        JS8Call (HF)Ham (General for most HF)Keyboard messaging over HF that works with weak signals and can store and relay messages across states.

        Set up a family Meshtastic net (no license)

        1. Buy one node per person plus one for a high spot at home (an attic or roof node greatly increases coverage). Make sure they're the 915 MHz / US versions.
        2. Install the free Meshtastic app now, while online. Pair each node to its owner's phone by Bluetooth.
        3. Set the region to US. Create a private channel with a shared key and add it to every family node.
        4. Mount the home node as high as possible with power (USB or a small solar panel).
        5. Test across your neighborhood. Range per hop varies from a few hundred yards in town to many miles between high points.

        Meshtastic complements voice radio; it doesn't replace it. Keep both in your PACE plan.

        Monthly practice drillsSkills fade unless you use them
        TroubleshootingCan't hear or can't be heard?
        • Can hear but not reach a repeater: wrong transmit tone, wrong offset direction, or too weak. Check tone and +/−; go higher or switch to high power.
        • Repeater "kerchunks" but no one answers: you're getting in. Call again later or try a net time.
        • Two radios on the same channel can't talk: privacy codes don't match, wide/narrow mismatch, or one radio is in frequency mode on a different frequency.
        • Constant hiss: raise squelch one step.
        • Audio is chopped or "picket-fencing": you're at the edge of range. Move a few feet or step out of the car.
        • Radio gets hot or SWR warning: bad antenna connection. Stop and check.
        • Stuck in weird mode: reset settings (Baofeng Menu 40 VFO reset keeps channels; ALL wipes them).

        Learn radio

        BasicsGMRSHamExam prep

        GMRS from zero: license, channels, power, repeaters and the rules. Checked against FCC Part 95E, Nov 2026.

        GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) is a licensed service on channels around 462 and 467 MHz, mostly for short-distance two-way voice with handhelds, mobiles and repeaters. Since 2017 it also allows short text messages and GPS locations. One license covers your whole immediate family, and there's no exam.

        Ready to test yourself? Take the practice quiz below the lessons.

        1 · Get your license18+, $35, 10 years, no exam
        1. Do it while you have internet. Go to the FCC's licensing site (fcc.gov → Licensing → ULS). Create an FCC Username and get an FRN (your FCC registration number) in CORES.
        2. In ULS License Manager, choose Apply for a New License and pick ZA – General Mobile Radio (GMRS).
        3. Answer the questions (it's FCC Form 605), pay the $35 fee, and submit.
        4. Your call sign appears in your ULS account once the license is granted. Write it on a label on every family radio, and add it on the Home tab so RELAY uses it.
        Who can apply
        Individuals 18 or older (not a representative of a foreign government).
        Who can talk on it
        You and your immediate family, any age: spouse, children, grandchildren, stepchildren, parents, grandparents, stepparents, brothers and sisters, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, and in-laws.
        Term
        10 years. Renew from 90 days before it expires up to the expiration date. After it expires, you need a new license.
        Where it's valid
        The 50 states, DC, and the US Caribbean and Pacific island areas.
        2 · Channels and power30 channels: what each group allows
        ChannelsFrequencies (MHz)Power limitWidth
        1–7462.5625–462.71255 W ERP20 kHz
        8–14467.5625–467.71250.5 W ERP (handhelds)12.5 kHz
        15–22462.5500–462.725050 W (mobile, base, repeater)20 kHz
        Repeater inputs467.5500–467.725050 W20 kHz
        • Channels 1–22 are shared with FRS (license-free) radios, so you'll hear FRS users there too.
        • No channel belongs to anyone. Everyone shares, so pick quiet channels and cooperate.
        • A typical handheld puts out about 5 W. A mobile on Ch 15–22 can run much more and reach farther.
        • Full channel list with notes: Channels.
        3 · RepeatersReach 20+ miles through a hilltop station
        • A GMRS repeater listens on a 467 MHz input and retransmits on the matching 462 MHz output (Ch 15–22), always +5 MHz apart.
        • Most need a tone (CTCSS or DCS) to open. Get it from the owner or a repeater directory such as myGMRS.com. Look it up while online and save it in your Radio Book.
        • Using someone else's repeater requires the owner's permission. Many are open to licensed users who ask; some are private.
        • Program it with the programming wizard, then test with a short call and your call sign.
        4 · Station ID and good habitsYour call sign, every 15 minutes
        • Identify with your call sign at the end of a transmission or conversation, and every 15 minutes during a long one. Voice in English is fine (Morse tone is also allowed).
        • Family members on your license use your call sign.
        • Listen before you talk. Keep it short and leave gaps so others can break in.
        • Use low power when you're close. It saves battery and keeps the channel clearer for others.
        • “Privacy” codes aren't private. A CTCSS or DCS code only filters what your radio hears; anyone without a code hears everything.
        • Practice the calls in the simulator.
        5 · What's not allowedThe rules people break most
        • No coded messages meant to hide meaning. Ordinary “10-codes” are allowed.
        • No advertising or selling goods or services. No political campaign ads.
        • No false or deceptive messages, and nothing tied to illegal activity.
        • No continuous or uninterrupted transmitting, except for immediate safety of life or property.
        • No connecting GMRS to the phone network or the internet to carry conversations. Networks may only be used to remote-control a repeater.
        • No non-emergency talking to ham stations.
        • Use a radio certified for GMRS (FCC Part 95E). A ham radio like the UV-5R isn't legal for GMRS transmit, even with a GMRS license.
        6 · Text and GPS dataAllowed since 2017, within limits
        • Short digital data, such as text messages and GPS location sharing, is allowed on GMRS. Radios like the BTECH GMRS-PRO do this between compatible units.
        • Data isn't allowed on the 467 MHz main channels (the repeater inputs).
        • Keep data brief, and use certified radios with built-in data features.
        GMRS course: practice quiz26 questions based on FCC Part 95E · not an FCC test

        GMRS has no license exam: you apply and pay the fee. This course makes sure you and your family know the rules you're agreeing to. The quiz is RELAY's own practice, based on FCC Part 95E, not an FCC test.

        The quiz needs JavaScript. The lessons are in Learn → GMRS from zero.

        Sources: 47 CFR Part 95 Subpart E (§§95.1705, 95.1733, 95.1749, 95.1751, 95.1767, 95.1773) on eCFR; FCC GMRS page; FCC Personal Service and Amateur fee table. Rules and fees can change; check fcc.gov when you apply.

        BasicsGMRSHamExam prep

        Amateur (ham) radio: Q-codes, Morse code and the HF bands that reach across the country.

        Ham radio needs an FCC amateur license, which means passing an exam. The entry-level Technician license gives you full VHF/UHF ham privileges (like 2 m and 70 cm repeaters) and some HF; General opens most of HF. Give your call sign every 10 minutes and at the end of a contact.

        Get ready for the exam in Learn → Exam prep. Repeater offsets are in Channels, and calls and nets are in Basics.

        HF bands: which works whenLong-distance radio for General-class hams

        HF signals bounce off the ionosphere, which changes with the time of day, season and the 11-year sunspot cycle. Rules of thumb:

        BandBest timeTypical reach
        160 m / 80 m (1.8 / 3.5–4 MHz)NightRegional by day (a few hundred miles), farther at night. Great for statewide emergency nets in the evening.
        60 m (5 MHz channels)Day and nightRegional; used for emergency coordination.
        40 m (7 MHz)Day and nightDaytime ~100–600 miles (NVIS); night: across the country and beyond. The workhorse emergency band.
        20 m (14 MHz)DaytimeWorldwide in daylight; Hurricane Watch Net 14.325.
        15 m / 10 m (21 / 28 MHz)Daytime, sunspot peaksWorldwide when the sun is active; dead at night and near solar minimum.

        NVIS (near-vertical incidence skywave): a low horizontal wire antenna (about 10–20 ft up) on 40 m or 80 m shoots signals almost straight up and fills in a 0–300 mile circle with no "skip zone". It's ideal for reaching your state's emergency nets when repeaters are down.

        Technicians can use HF Morse code (CW) on parts of 80, 40 and 15 m, and voice on 10 m (28.3–28.5). Most HF voice needs a General license.

        Two-week Technician study planAbout 30–45 minutes a day
        DayDo this
        1Read "About the exam". Get your FRN at the FCC CORES site (free). Read lesson T1 (Rules).
        2Practice T1 until you score 80%+. Learn the Technician band chart below.
        3Lesson + practice T2 (Operating) and T8 (Modes).
        4Lesson + practice T3 (Radio waves). Memorize λ = 300 / f.
        5Lesson T5 (Electricity). Practice Ohm's law and power math with the cheat sheet.
        6Lesson + practice T6 (Components) and T7 (Station equipment).
        7Lesson + practice T9 (Antennas) and T0 (Safety). First mock exam.
        8Review missed questions. Re-read the weakest lesson.
        9–11One mock exam a day + review missed questions. Find an exam session and register.
        12–13Mock exams. Goal: 3 passes in a row at 85%+.
        14Light review of the cheat sheet. Pack your exam-day kit. Sleep well.

        Memory tricks: read the correct answer out loud; make up a silly sentence for each number (e.g., "Two meters, 144 to 148, two gross"); explain a topic to someone else. Short daily sessions beat one long cram.

        Technician lessons

        One plain-language lesson per Technician topic. Read the lesson, then quiz that topic above.

        T1 · FCC rules (biggest topic)Licenses, privileges, IDs, what's allowed
        • The FCC regulates US amateur radio under Part 97. Internationally, the ITU sets the framework.
        • Purpose of ham radio: emergency communications, advancing radio technology, improving skills, building a pool of trained operators and technicians, and international goodwill.
        • License term: 10 years. Grace period: 2 years to renew after it expires (no transmitting while expired).
        • You may transmit once your call sign appears in the FCC ULS database. Keep your mailing address and email current with the FCC.
        • Identify with your call sign at least every 10 minutes and at the end of a contact, in English (or Morse).
        • Control operator: the licensed person responsible for transmissions. The station licensee is also responsible. The control operator's license class sets the privileges used.
        • Not allowed: music, obscene or indecent language, codes or encryption meant to hide meaning, business for profit, broadcasting to the public, false signals.
        • Allowed one-way: Morse practice, bulletins for amateurs, beacons, remote control of model craft (telecommand).
        • Third-party traffic: passing messages for a non-ham. Internationally, only with countries that have an agreement with the US.
        • Secondary allocation: on some bands (e.g., 70 cm), hams must not interfere with primary users and must accept interference from them.
        • Emergencies: when life or property is in immediate danger and normal systems aren't available, any means of communication may be used.
        • Exams: given by 3 Volunteer Examiners (VEs) under a VEC.
        • Power: up to 1,500 W PEP in general; 200 W PEP in Technician HF segments. Always use the minimum power necessary.
        Technician band privileges chartMemorize this for T1
        BandFrequenciesTechnician use
        80 m3.525–3.600CW only, 200 W
        40 m7.025–7.125CW only, 200 W
        15 m21.025–21.200CW only, 200 W
        10 m28.000–28.300CW, RTTY/data, 200 W
        10 m28.300–28.500SSB voice + CW, 200 W

        2 m144–148All modes (144.0–144.1 CW only)

        70 cm420–450All modes
        33 cm902–928All modes
        23 cm1240–1300All modes

        Trick: "2 m = 144–148, 70 cm = 420–450, 6 m = 50–54." The band name is roughly the wavelength: 300 / 146 ≈ 2 m.

        T2 · Operating proceduresRepeaters, calling, nets, emergency groups
        • Calling frequencies: 146.520 (2 m) and 446.000 (70 cm) FM simplex.
        • Repeater offsets: 2 m = 600 kHz, 1.25 m = 1.6 MHz, 70 cm = 5 MHz.
        • CTCSS / PL tone: a sub-audible tone the repeater needs to hear. Can't access a repeater you can hear? Check tone and offset.
        • Reverse: listen on the repeater's input to see if you can talk simplex. If you can, move to simplex and free the repeater.
        • On a repeater, just say your call sign to show you're listening. CQ means "calling any station" (used on HF/simplex).
        • Answering a call: their call sign, then yours.
        • Band plans are voluntary guidelines beyond FCC rules.
        • Nets: net control runs it. In emergencies, stay quiet unless you have essential traffic.
        • ARES (ARRL volunteers) and RACES (government emergency management) are the main emergency groups.
        • Radiogram: the "check" is the word count of the message text.
        • Digital voice: DMR uses talkgroups and a code plug (programming file); a hotspot links your radio to internet networks.
        • Q-signals: QRM = interference from others, QRN = static, QSY = change frequency, QTH = location, QSL = I confirm.
        T3 · Radio waves and propagationWavelength, bands, how signals travel
        • Wavelength (m) = 300 / frequency (MHz). Higher frequency = shorter wavelength.
        • HF 3–30 MHz, VHF 30–300 MHz, UHF 300–3,000 MHz.
        • Radio waves travel at the speed of light (300,000,000 m/s). They're made of electric and magnetic fields at right angles.
        • Polarization: vertical for FM/repeaters; horizontal for long-distance SSB/CW on VHF/UHF. Mismatched polarization loses a lot of signal.
        • Line of sight: VHF/UHF are blocked by hills, buildings and wet foliage. The radio horizon is slightly beyond the visual horizon because the atmosphere bends the waves.
        • Multipath: reflections that arrive at different times cause fading and errors. A mobile signal fluttering is picket fencing.
        • Knife-edge diffraction: signals bend over sharp edges like ridgelines.
        • Tropospheric ducting: temperature inversions carry VHF/UHF hundreds of miles.
        • Sporadic E: summer openings on 6 m and 10 m. Meteor scatter: best on 6 m. Aurora: signals sound buzzy and distorted.
        • Ionosphere: HF signals bounce (skip) off it. The D layer absorbs low HF in daytime. The sunspot cycle is about 11 years; more sunspots = better high HF.
        • UHF slips into buildings better (short wavelength fits through openings).
        T4 · Station setup and radio controlsMobile wiring, digital interfaces, receiver controls
        • Mobile radios above a few watts: run fused power leads directly to the battery, not the cigarette lighter. Use heavy enough wire.
        • Alternator whine rises and falls with engine speed.
        • Digital modes (FT8 etc.): a computer sound card interface carries audio in/out and keys PTT.
        • Squelch mutes noise. VFO tunes any frequency. Memory channels store settings.
        • RIT / clarifier shifts receive frequency only.
        • Filters: CW ≈ 500 Hz, SSB ≈ 2.4 kHz. Narrower = less noise.
        • Too much mic gain or deviation on FM = distorted audio and interference to nearby channels.
        • Transverter: converts a radio's signals to another band.
        T5 · Electricity and mathUnits, Ohm's law, power, decibels, prefixes
        QuantityUnitSymbol
        Voltage (EMF)VoltE (or V)
        CurrentAmpereI
        Resistance / impedanceOhmR / Z
        PowerWattP
        CapacitanceFaradC
        InductanceHenryL
        FrequencyHertzf
        • Ohm's law: E = I × R. Cover the one you want: I = E / R, R = E / I.
        • Power: P = E × I. So I = P / E, E = P / I.
        • Series circuits: same current. Parallel: same voltage.
        • DC flows one way (batteries). AC alternates (US mains 60 Hz).
        • Decibels: ×2 power = +3 dB, ×4 = +6 dB, ×10 = +10 dB, ½ = −3 dB.
        • Short circuit = unintended low-resistance path (big current). Open circuit = a break (no current).
        • Conductors: copper, aluminum. Insulators: glass, plastic, ceramic.
        T6 · Electronic componentsWhat each part does
        PartWhat it does
        ResistorOpposes current. A potentiometer is a variable resistor (volume knob).
        CapacitorStores energy in an electric field.
        Inductor (coil)Stores energy in a magnetic field.
        DiodeCurrent flows one way. The band marks the cathode. Used in rectifiers (AC → DC).
        LEDDiode that gives off light.
        TransistorAmplifies or switches. BJT: emitter, base, collector. FET: gate, drain, source.
        RelayElectrically controlled switch.
        TransformerChanges AC voltage levels.
        Fuse / breakerOpens on overcurrent.
        Voltage regulatorHolds output voltage steady.
        LC tuned circuitResonates at one frequency; selects or rejects it.
        Integrated circuitMany components on one chip.
        Solar (photovoltaic) cellConverts light to DC electricity.

        Batteries: rechargeable = NiMH (1.2 V/cell), Li-ion (≈3.6–3.7 V/cell), lead-acid (12.6 V full for a "12 V" battery). Not rechargeable: carbon-zinc, standard alkaline.

        The exam includes schematic-symbol questions using diagrams. Learn the symbols for resistor (zigzag), capacitor (two plates), inductor (coils), diode (triangle + bar), transistor, battery (long/short lines), ground, antenna, switch and lamp from the official pool's figures.

        T7 · Station equipment and troubleshootingMeters, SWR, interference, soldering
        • Transceiver = transmitter + receiver.
        • Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel. Turn power OFF before measuring resistance.
        • SWR meter goes between the transmitter and the antenna feed line. 1:1 is perfect.
        • Antenna tuner matches impedance; it doesn't make a bad antenna radiate better.
        • Dummy load: a 50 Ω resistor that absorbs power for testing without radiating.
        • Interference to a neighbor's TV: if it happens on your fundamental frequency, filter at the TV (high-pass filter, common-mode choke). Harmonics: low-pass filter at your transmitter. Check your own station first.
        • Ferrite chokes reduce RF on cables.
        • Distorted audio reports: RF feedback, low battery voltage, mic gain too high.
        • Soldering: rosin-core solder for electronics. A cold joint looks dull and grainy.
        • Oscilloscope shows waveforms. Sensitivity = hearing weak signals; selectivity = separating close signals.
        • Duplexer lets a repeater transmit and receive on one antenna. Mixer creates sum and difference frequencies.
        T8 · Modes, satellites and activitiesFM, SSB, CW, digital, space
        ModeBandwidthUsed for
        CW (Morse)~150 HzNarrowest; gets through noise
        SSB voice~3 kHzLong distance, weak signal. USB on 10 m and above; LSB below 10 MHz
        AM voice~6 kHzAircraft, broadcast, some hams
        FM voice5–15 kHzLocal VHF/UHF and repeaters
        Fast-scan TV~6 MHz70 cm and higher only
        • Satellites: uplink = to the satellite, downlink = from it. "Mode U/V" = UHF up, VHF down. Doppler shift changes the frequency as it passes. Use the minimum power needed. Technicians can work satellites and the ISS.
        • APRS (144.390 MHz): position, weather and short messages.
        • FT8: weak-signal digital with 15-second slots; needs accurate computer time.
        • Winlink: email over radio.
        • Fox hunting: finding a hidden transmitter with a directional antenna.
        • Grid locator: like FN20; used in contests and digital modes. EME = bouncing signals off the Moon.
        • Contests: exchange only the minimum info, quickly.
        T9 · Antennas and feed linesLengths, types, coax, connectors
        • Half-wave dipole length (feet) ≈ 468 / f (MHz). 6 m ≈ 112 inches.
        • Quarter-wave vertical (feet) ≈ 234 / f (MHz). 2 m ≈ 19 inches.
        • A dipole radiates best broadside (perpendicular) to the wire.
        • Yagi: directional beam. Driven element is fed; reflector behind, directors in front.
        • 5/8-wave whip: more gain at a low angle than a 1/4-wave. Rubber duck: convenient but inefficient.
        • Shorten an antenna → resonant frequency goes up. Lengthen → goes down. Loading coils electrically lengthen short antennas.
        • Gain comes from focusing energy in some directions.
        • Coax: 50 Ω is standard. Loss rises with frequency and length; moisture increases loss. Air-insulated hardline is lowest loss.
        • Connectors: PL-259/SO-239 common on HF/VHF; Type N low-loss and weatherproof at UHF and up; SMA on handhelds.
        • Ladder line: balanced, very low loss.
        • Antenna analyzer: measures SWR/impedance across frequencies.
        T0 · SafetyElectrical, towers, lightning, RF exposure
        • Electrical: current through the body is what injures. Never use a fuse larger than specified. A GFCI trips when current leaks to ground.
        • Batteries: lead-acid gives off explosive hydrogen when charging (ventilate). Lithium can catch fire if shorted, damaged or charged/discharged too fast.
        • Generators: outside only (carbon monoxide). Use a transfer switch; never backfeed house wiring.
        • Antennas & towers: keep them where they can't fall onto power lines. Climb with a harness and hard hat, with a helper on the ground. Never climb a crank-up tower unless it's fully retracted or blocked.
        • Lightning: bond all grounds together with short, direct connections; use lightning arrestors at the entry point; disconnect antennas when not in use.
        • RF exposure: RF is non-ionizing; its hazard is heating tissue. Limits are strictest from 30–300 MHz. Exposure depends on frequency, power, distance, antenna pattern and duty cycle (less transmit time = less average exposure). Reduce it by moving antennas away or up, or lowering power. Stations must be evaluated for RF exposure.

        During the exam: answer the ones you know first, then come back. Watch for "which is NOT…" questions. If two answers look right, pick the more complete one. Change an answer only if you're sure.

        After you passFrom paper to call sign
        1. The VE team gives you a CSCE certificate and submits your application.
        2. The FCC emails you a link to pay the $35 fee. Pay it within the deadline in the email (about 10 days) or the application is dismissed.
        3. Watch the FCC ULS for your new call sign (often within days). You can transmit once it appears.
        4. Program your local repeaters, say hello, and check into a weekly net.
        5. Join a local club and ARES. Then start on the General exam for HF privileges.

        App status

        NATO alphabet

        The phonetic alphabet every radio service uses. Spell call signs, names and addresses so nothing gets misheard.

        Spell it with NATO words

          The speller needs JavaScript. The full alphabet is below.

          NATO letters A–Z

          Pronunciation as NATO writes it. Morse code under each word. Tap a letter to hear it.

          NATO numbers 0–9

          Say each digit on its own. 146.520 = “wun fow-er six point fife too zee-ro”. Some numbers have a radio pronunciation, like tree, fife and nin-er, so they aren't confused (nine can sound like the German “nein”).

          How to use it on the radio“I spell”, call signs, examples
          • Say “I spell” before spelling a word, then the code words: “Oak, I spell: Oscar Alfa Kilo.”
          • Give your call sign phonetically when signals are weak, checking into a net, or when asked: KX4ABC = “Kilo X-ray Fow-er Alfa Bravo Charlie”.
          • Spell anything that could be misheard: street names, last names, medicines, grid squares.
          • Times are 24-hour, one digit at a time when it matters: 3:30 PM = “fifteen-thirty” or “wun fife tree zee-ro”.
          • Use only the standard words. Made-up words (“A as in apple”) slow everyone down and confuse listeners from other places.
          • Why the odd spellings? Alfa and Juliett are spelled so speakers of other languages say them correctly: “ph” isn't read as “f” everywhere, and a single final “t” can go silent in French.

          More: Learn → Basics (prowords, Q-codes, Morse) · Practice calls.

          History of the NATO alphabet1927 to 1956: five alphabets before the one we use

          The alphabet in use today took effect in 1956 and within a few years became the single phonetic alphabet for military, civil aviation and amateur radio worldwide. It went through several versions first.

          1. 1927 · ITU, the first international alphabet

            The International Telecommunication Union published the first phonetic alphabet recognized internationally. Most words were cities and countries.

            Amsterdam, Baltimore, Canada, Denmark, Eddystone, Francisco, Gibraltar, Hanover, Italy, Jerusalem, Kimberley, Liverpool, Madagascar, Neufchatel, Ontario, Portugal, Quebec, Rivoli, Santiago, Tokio, Uruguay, Victoria, Washington, Xantippe, Yokohama, Zululand

          2. 1932 · ITU revision

            The ITU replaced several words; the list was still mostly place names.

            Amsterdam, Baltimore, Casablanca, Danemark, Edison, Florida, Gallipoli, Havana, Italia, Jerusalem, Kilogramme, Liverpool, Madagascar, New York, Oslo, Paris, Quebec, Roma, Santiago, Tripoli, Upsala, Valencia, Washington, Xanthippe, Yokohama, Zürich

          3. 1941 · “Able Baker” (US military)

            The US adopted one Joint Army/Navy alphabet for all its military branches, named after its first two words. Britain's Royal Air Force took it up two years later.

            Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog, Easy, Fox, George, How, Item, Jig, King, Love, Mike, Nan, Oboe, Peter, Queen, Roger, Sugar, Tare, Uncle, Victor, William, X-ray, Yoke, Zebra

          4. 1951 · IATA (civil aviation)

            Earlier alphabets were criticized as too English. The International Air Transport Association proposed words built from sounds common to English, French and Spanish. It took effect on 1 November 1951, for civil aviation only.

            Alfa, Bravo, Coca, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Gold, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Metro, Nectar, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Union, Victor, Whiskey, eXtra, Yankee, Zulu

          5. 1956 · NATO, the universal alphabet

            Militaries kept using Able Baker while airlines used IATA, so civil and military authorities agreed on one alphabet. In the mid-1950s NATO, led by the United Kingdom and the United States, reviewed the IATA list and proposed changing five words: Coca, Metro, Nectar, Union and eXtra. The proposal went to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with debate over Nectar or November for N.

            On 8 April 1955 NATO's Standing Group said the alphabet would take effect for NATO on 1 January 1956 whether or not ICAO approved. Allied militaries waited for ICAO, which approved it with November. On 21 February 1956 the Allies were told it would take effect in NATO on 1 March 1956.

            The ITU formally adopted it a few years later. Because NATO led the final revision, it became known as the NATO phonetic alphabet.

            Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu

          Source: NATO, “History of the NATO phonetic alphabet” and the NATO phonetic alphabet poster (nato.int); NATO Archives documents SGWM-762-54, SGM-0217-55 and SGM-0156-56.

          Tools

          Readiness checks, settings and calculators. Everything works offline.

          Offline readiness checkReal tests on this device, not a checklist

          Runs actual checks: storage, data integrity, install state. Results: PASS WARN FAIL NOT TESTED.

          Manual airplane-mode test (do this once)

          1. Open RELAY the way you'll use it in an emergency (home-screen app or saved file).
          2. Turn on Airplane Mode and Wi-Fi off. Close RELAY completely.
          3. Reopen it. Check Home, Channels, Radios, Learn and More all open, and your plan is still there.
          4. Restart the phone, still in Airplane Mode, and repeat.
          5. If anything fails, keep the downloaded file as a backup and export your plan.

          Phones can clear website storage when space runs low or after weeks without use, especially on iPhone. "Protect my data" asks the browser to keep it, but no browser guarantees it. Export your plan regularly.

          Data packs & sourcesWhat's stored, when it was verified

          Everything ships inside RELAY itself, so an update replaces all of it at once. A new version only takes over after it has fully downloaded; until then the old version keeps working. Integrity is checked with a SHA-256 fingerprint. That detects damaged data, but it doesn't prove who published it.

          Uses typical wire velocity (~95%). Cut a little long, then trim while watching SWR.

          Enter coordinates (decimal degrees; west and south are negative).

          Range estimator (line of sight)How far can two antennas see each other?

          This is the best case over flat ground. Hills, buildings and trees cut it down; high ground adds to it. A repeater on a 1,000 ft hill sees ~45 miles.

          Coax loss calculatorHow much power reaches your antenna?
          Battery runtime estimatorHow long will my handheld last?

          Rough estimate using typical handheld current draw (transmit ~0.8–1.5 A, receive ~0.15 A, standby ~0.05 A at 7.4 V). Real results vary by radio, age and temperature.

          Keep RELAY on your phone offlineDo this now, while you have internet

          Test it: turn on Airplane Mode and open RELAY. If it opens, you're set.

          Option A: the downloaded file (simplest)

          • Android: save relay-radio-guide.html to Downloads. Open it with Chrome (or Firefox). Bookmark it or add it to your home screen from the browser menu.
          • iPhone: save the file to the Files app (On My iPhone). Tapping it shows a preview with all the guide content. For the full app (search, calculators, saved notes), open it in a file-browser app that runs web pages, or use Option B.

          Option B: install as an app (best on iPhone)

          1. Upload the relay-app folder to a free static host (Netlify Drop, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages).
          2. Open that link in Safari (iPhone) or Chrome (Android).
          3. iPhone: Share → Add to Home Screen. Android: menu → Install app.
          4. Open it once from the home screen while online. It stores itself on the phone and then works with no internet.

          Notes and checklists are saved in the browser you use. If you switch browsers or clear website data, export your Radio Book first.

          Also print the Frequencies tab and your family plan. Paper never runs out of battery.
